This article is based on the video “Chinese and American Tech Stocks Crash! Why You Should Stay Calm as U.S. Stocks Fall but Never Buy the Dip in A-Shares — How Should Ordinary People Invest?” by Lao Zhou Hengmei (November 5, 2026). Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=l7YOTaKV8gc

Lately, tech stocks in the U.S. and China have crashed at the same time. Wall Street is starting to wonder whether AI is a bubble; the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 are sliding together, and Chinese tech stocks have been hit even harder. Faced with all this, what should ordinary people do? Why do most retail investors make money in bull markets and lose it all in bear markets? And what are the most important strategies, mindsets, and methods an ordinary person should actually master?

Bull-Market Gurus, Bear-Market Dogs

Most people lose money in the stock market for one simple reason: they think they can predict it.

In a bull market, everyone's a genius. Buy any tech stock and it goes up; group chats are full of people posting their gains, and making money feels easy. But the moment a bear market arrives, almost everyone is exposed: the profits evaporate, and then some. Why? Because in a bull market, the money comes from the market, not from skill. In a bear market, what you lose is exactly the skill you thought you had.

Lao Zhou has warned about this for a long time: don't think you can predict the market. Nobody can say how the market will move in the short term. The people who spend every day predicting whether tomorrow goes up or down, whether this is the bottom — they almost always end up losing. Predicting the market is itself the biggest reason retail investors lose money.

Long-Term Thinking: A Crash Is Nothing to Panic About

Why is a stock market crash nothing to panic about? Because investing isn't about the next year or two.

In the short term, markets going up and down is completely normal. No matter how brutal a crash looks, on a timeline of ten or twenty years it's often just a blip. What decides whether you end up making money isn't how many crashes you dodged — it's whether you stayed in the market long enough, and whether you kept buying when things were cheap.

Long-term thinking comes down to one sentence: don't let short-term swings drag you around. Panic-selling in a crash and chasing rallies in a bull market — that's how retail investors usually die. But if you believe the economy grows over the long run and quality assets appreciate over time, a crash is just a chance to buy the same things at a lower price.

Why Ordinary People Shouldn't Pick Individual Stocks

Picking individual stocks sounds exciting, but ordinary people shouldn't touch it.

First, it takes professional skill. You have to read financial statements, follow industries, judge management teams, assess valuations, and track every change at the companies you own. Ordinary people work all day and get a couple of hours in the evening — how are they supposed to compete with full-time fund managers and institutions? You're behind on information, behind on research, and behind on time from the very start.

Second, individual stocks are far too risky. One black swan at a single company and the stock can halve or even get delisted. Put your money in a handful of individual stocks and you're betting your livelihood on luck. And luck is not something you can count on.

So the best thing ordinary people can do is give up the fantasy of “getting rich by picking stocks.” You won't find the next ten-bagger, and there's no need to lose sleep over it. The point of investing isn't to get rich overnight — it's to grow your money steadily over the long term.

Index Funds: The Simplest, Most Effective Strategy for Ordinary People

For ordinary people, the simplest and most effective strategy is index funds.

The Nasdaq, the S&P 500, QQQ, SPY — these funds track the whole market, not a single company. Buy one and you've effectively bought the best companies in America. A single company can go bankrupt, but the market as a whole trends upward over the long run. Diversification takes the individual-stock risk off the table.

The beauty of index funds is that they're simple, cheap, and they work. No stock picking, no staring at charts all day, no worrying about landmines. Just buy regularly, hold for the long term, and let time do the rest. Warren Buffett has publicly recommended index funds to ordinary people many times — not as a platitude, but as his most honest advice.

Why You'll Never Become Buffett

Plenty of people object: Buffett made his fortune buying stocks too — why can't I become him?

The answer is simple: you'll never become Buffett, and it's not because you buy index funds. It's because you don't have Buffett's advantages: enormous capital, top-tier information channels, decades of experience, extraordinary mental discipline, and an entire team working for him. When he buys a company, he can send people to investigate on the ground, negotiate with management, and deploy billions to buy the dip when the market panics. And you? You have a phone and two hours after work.

Seeing that clearly isn't meant to make you feel small — it's meant to wake you up. Don't dream of copying Buffett's stock-picking legend, and don't imagine you're the one-in-a-million genius. Ordinary people should use ordinary methods: regular index-fund investing, held for the long term. That's the right road for the rest of us.

Invest 2,000 Yuan a Month — 3.94 Million in 20 Years

Most people have no intuitive feel for the power of compounding. The video walks through the math: invest 2,000 yuan a month, keep it up for 20 years, and by one estimate you'd end up with 3.94 million yuan.

Two thousand a month doesn't sound like much. That's 24,000 a year, and 480,000 in principal over 20 years. But if that money stays in the market, compounding year after year, it can snowball into 3.94 million. That's compounding: money making money, interest on interest, and the longer the time, the bigger the snowball.

The key word is “persistence.” Dollar-cost averaging isn't about buying once — it's about buying every single month, rain or shine, up or down. When prices rise, keep buying. When they fall, buy even more: the same money buys more shares, and when the market recovers, the gains are magnified. Most people fail at dollar-cost averaging not because the method is wrong, but because they can't stick with it: they want to sell when prices rise and they're too scared to buy when prices fall — and they're right back to chasing rallies and panic-selling dips.

Compounding needs time, and it needs discipline. Twenty years is a long time — but that's exactly why it's worth it.

U.S. Stocks Are Investing; A-Shares Are a Casino

U.S. stocks are investing; A-shares are a casino. It sounds harsh, but that's the video's verdict, stated plainly.

The logic of U.S. stocks is investing: you're buying a company's future, a share of long-term economic growth. The Nasdaq and the S&P 500 trend upward over time because behind them are some of the best companies in the world generating real profits. You can stay calm when they fall because you know they'll come back over the long run.

A-shares are a completely different story. This latest bloodbath in Chinese tech stocks proves once again that they're no place for ordinary people to buy the dip. The video urges viewers again and again not to touch A-shares — not because there are no good companies in the market, but because the system and the rules are stacked against retail investors. In A-shares, retail investors face a market where the rules aren't even.

Worse Than a Casino? The System Behind A-Shares

Why is it fair to say A-shares are worse than a casino? Because at least a casino has transparent rules — you place your bet and accept the outcome. The structural problems behind A-shares mean retail investors can lose without even understanding how.

The video goes into the structural truth behind A-shares. The system was never designed to protect small investors in the first place: disclosure rules, delisting mechanisms, rules on major shareholders selling down their stakes, the financing structure — at every turn, the setup works against retail investors. When retail investors can't make money in A-shares, it's not bad luck. The system just isn't on their side.

What's crueler still is that for many ordinary Chinese people with no other investment options, there's almost nowhere else legitimate to put their money. Keep it in the bank and inflation eats it; put it in A-shares and get fleeced. The video ends on that point too: ordinary people with no investment channels — what else can they do besides get fleeced in A-shares? It's a question worth thinking hard about.

Conclusion: How Ordinary People Should Invest

Back to the original question: with tech stocks crashing in both the U.S. and China, what should ordinary people do?

The answer is actually simple, and plain: don't try to predict the market, don't pick individual stocks, and don't dream of becoming Buffett. Put your money in index funds, invest a fixed amount every month, stick with it for the long term, and let compounding do the work. Stay calm when U.S. stocks crash — they'll come back over time. As for A-shares, leave them alone, and don't even think about buying the dip.

Investing isn't gambling, and getting rich doesn't happen overnight. The most valuable thing ordinary people can master isn't the skill of predicting ups and downs — it's the mindset of long-term thinking and the discipline of regular investing. That's how you ride out bull and bear markets alike, and actually grow your money.
excerpt_en: U.S. and Chinese tech stocks are crashing at the same time. Here's why most retail investors make money in bull markets and give it all back in bear markets — and what ordinary people should actually do.
